title: Twice-recycled fuel loaded into BN-800 fast neutron reactor
html:
Russia's state nuclear corporation, Rosatom, said it was the first time a commercial high-capacity reactor had proved the viability of a closed fuel cycle concept.

When a fuel assembly is irradiated during its time in an operating reactor, it generates plutonium within the fuel which can be recovered after the assembly is removed. That plutonium can be used again in MOX (mixed oxide) fuel - a cycle which in theory can be repeated many times over. In this case, plutonium from used MOX fuel has been recovered and used to make more fuel for the same unit.

Rosatom said: "A one-step process had been tested before: irradiated fuel from conventional thermal reactors has been processed and loaded into a fast reactor within fresh fuel, without a second recycling stage. But that did not unlock the full potential of multi-cycle recycling - the approach that removes the uranium-resource ceiling and creates a virtually inexhaustible energy source."

Director General of Rosatom Alexey Likhachev said: "Today, in closing the nuclear fuel cycle around fast reactors, we have moved from theory to practice. By overcoming this next technological milestone, we are proving the viability of a 'renewable' nuclear energy model. It will allow us to meet growing electricity demands without a proportional increase in the strain on natural resources or in radioactive waste volumes. The successful operation of this unique fuel assembly in BN-800 is a direct step toward the technological readiness of future Gen IV reactors, including the serial BN-1200M unit, which will go online in the coming decade."

Rosatom said that the new experimental fuel assembly was produced using an optimised plutonium-recovery process which cut the total number of processing steps while fully preserving fuel quality, making recycling more economical.

The Beloyarsk 4 BN-800 reactor is a sodium-cooled fast reactor which produces about 820 MWe. It was brought to minimum controlled power for the first time in June 2014, and connected to the grid on 10 December 2015. The reactor entered commercial operation on 31 October 2016. It was fully loaded with MOX fuel in September 2022 and became the first such facility to complete a year operating on MOX fuel. MOX fuel is manufactured from plutonium recovered from used reactor fuel, mixed with depleted uranium which is a by-product from uranium enrichment.
summary: Recycled uranium-plutonium MOX fuel, manufactured using plutonium extracted from a MOX fuel assembly which had already completed a full cycle, has been loaded into the Beloyarsk Nuclear Power Plant's BN-800 fast…
